Updated for Windows 11 25H2 on 08-10-2026. Tested on Enterprise x64.

After replacing your hosts file with this one on Windows 11 only, Virus and Threat Protection will report the hosts file has been hijacked, and you will need to allow it on the device.

Once the hosts file has been replaced, open a CMD prompt with elevated rights and run ipconfig /flushdns. A reboot is not required.

**Summary generated by Claude AI on 08-13-2026.**

## Results

### Domain reach: tweaked vs. untweaked (before any blocking)

Across both baseline (pre-hosts-file) captures, **248 unique domains** were contacted in total between the two machines.

| Machine | Domains contacted | Domains *not* contacted |
|---|---|---|
| **Tweaks VM** | 64 (25.8%) | 184 (74.2%) |
| **No-tweaks VM** | 232 (93.5%) | 16 (6.5%) |

The untweaked machine reached out to a large block of third-party ad-tech/tracking domains — real-time ad exchanges, identity-sync/data-broker services, and device-fingerprinting services (e.g. Xandr/AppNexus, Rubicon Project, PubMatic, OpenX, Criteo, Taboola, Adobe Audience Manager, comScore, ThreatMetrix) — that **never appeared at all** on the tweaked machine.

### Domain classification (for router/device-level blocking)

All 248 domains were categorized:

| Classification | Count | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Safe to block** | 132 | Third-party ad-tech/trackers, Microsoft's own advertising/telemetry, or optional content (MSN/Bing/Widgets, Bing Maps/Weather) |
| **Do not block** | 63 | Core infrastructure — Windows Update, Delivery Optimization, Microsoft Store, Xbox/Game Pass, sign-in |
| **Caution** | 35 | Shared Microsoft/Azure infrastructure (Front Door health probes, SmartScreen security checks, static CDNs) — low benefit or some functional risk to blocking |
| **Depends** | 11 | Office/Teams/Outlook — block only if those apps aren't used |
| **N/A** | 7 | Local network discovery (mDNS, WPAD, NetBIOS) — not real blockable internet domains |

### What we explicitly wanted to block

Third-party advertising and tracking networks, and Microsoft's own advertising/telemetry endpoints not required for core OS function.

### What we explicitly wanted to preserve

- **Windows Update** (including Delivery Optimization and certificate trust list downloads)
- **Microsoft Store** (catalog, licensing, update infrastructure)
- **Xbox app / Game Pass** (explicitly in active use)
- **Steam and other game clients** (excluded from testing/blocking entirely by request)

### Hosts-file deployment and verification

A device-level hosts file (`C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts`) was built containing all 132 "safe to block" domains, each pointed to `0.0.0.0`, grouped by category with comments. Deployed and verified on three machines:

| Machine | Result |
|---|---|
| **Tweaks VM** | 26/26 previously-confirmed-active blocklist domains fully blocked (100%) |
| **No-tweaks VM** | 127/129 previously-confirmed-active blocklist domains blocked (98.4%); 2 leaked through (`www.msn.com`, `aa.online-metrix.net`) — file itself was verified byte-for-byte correct with no formatting errors, so the leak is suspected to be a boot-timing race (Edge auto-launching before the hosts file fully reloads), not a bad entry |
| **Main desktop PC** (daily-use machine, tweaks + hosts file) | 0 blocklist domains leaked; Windows Update, Microsoft Store, and the full Xbox/Game Pass sign-in stack all confirmed still resolving normally |

On all three machines, no Windows Update, Microsoft Store, or Xbox functionality was broken by the block list.

## Known limitations

- **The hosts file has no wildcard support.** At least one tracker (ThreatMetrix / `aa.online-metrix.net`) generates a new random subdomain prefix each session specifically to defeat static blocklists — a device-level hosts file can only ever catch the exact strings already seen, not future variants. A wildcard-capable network tool (e.g. Pi-hole, AdGuard Home) would close this gap.
- **Hosts-file blocking is per-device**, not network-wide — it has to be applied and maintained separately on every machine, unlike a router/DNS-server-level block.
- **Steam was intentionally not tested** and is not included in either the domain list or the hosts file, per an explicit decision to avoid any risk to game downloads/updates.
- **Domain coverage reflects only what was observed during the capture windows used** (up to 45 minutes per run) — infrequent or long-interval background check-ins may not have been captured, so the list is not guaranteed exhaustive.

## Bottom line

The tweaks meaningfully reduce Windows' contact surface — the untweaked machine reaches roughly 3.5x more unique domains than the tweaked one, largely driven by third-party ad-tech that's absent entirely from the tweaked install. The resulting hosts-file blocklist has been validated on two VMs and one real daily-driver desktop with a 100% success rate on protecting Windows Update, Microsoft Store, and Xbox functionality, and a 98–100% success rate at actually blocking the targeted domains.
